content.tldr: Plaintext refers specifically to unencrypted input awaiting mathematical transformation by a cryptographic cipher, whereas cleartext refers to any unencrypted data transmitted or stored in human-readable form.
content.simple_explanation: While frequently used interchangeably in informal dialogue, security engineering makes a precise distinction. Plaintext is a cryptographic term describing the raw operand fed into an encryption algorithm (or produced by a decryption algorithm). Cleartext is an architectural and networking term describing unencrypted, unprotected communications (such as legacy HTTP, Telnet, or FTP traffic) that can be intercepted by network sniffers.
content.real_world_example: A typed corporate document resting on a desktop is cleartext; when you feed that document into an AES encryption engine, the algorithm treats the document as its plaintext input.
content.why_it_matters_and_pitfalls: Logging cleartext sensitive credentials (API keys, passwords, health data) into production log aggregators creates severe compliance and data exfiltration liabilities. Cleartext network protocols must be prohibited in zero trust architectures.
